content: Tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) is an isoenzyme of tryptophan hydroxylase, and in humans, it is encoded by the TPH1 gene. This enzyme was first identified in 1988 as being responsible for the synthesis of serotonin. At the time, it was believed that there was only one TPH gene. However, in 2003, a second form of the enzyme, TPH2, was discovered in the mouse, rat, and human brain. Consequently, the original TPH was renamed TPH1. Tryptophan hydroxylases catalyze the biopterin-dependent monooxygenation of tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP). This intermediate is subsequently decarboxylated to produce serotonin, also known as 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), a key neurotransmitter. TPH1 is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of serotonin. Its expression is restricted to specific tissues, including raphe neurons, pinealocytes, mast cells, mononuclear leukocytes, beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, and enterochromaffin cells in the intestine and pancreas. Tryptophan hydroxylase plays a critical role in the synthesis of indoleamine neurotransmitters and related compounds in the body and brain. These include serotonin, melatonin, tryptamine, N-methyltryptamine, and N,N-dimethyltryptamine. TPH1 is expressed in peripheral tissues but not in the brain. Despite this, variations in the TPH1 gene have been studied for their potential effects on brain-related traits, such as personality characteristics and neuropsychiatric disorders. For instance, a 1998 study found an association between a polymorphism in the TPH1 gene and impulsive-aggressive behavior, while a 2001 case-control study found no link between TPH1 polymorphisms and Alzheimer’s disease. A specific human mutation in the TPH1 gene, known as A218C, located in intron 7, has been strongly associated with schizophrenia. Introns are non-coding regions of DNA that do not directly encode the amino acid sequence of proteins. Historically, introns were considered junk DNA with no functional purpose. However, the association of an intron mutation with schizophrenia highlights the potential importance of introns in processes such as transcription, translation, or other, possibly unknown, mechanisms involved in protein production from DNA.
